title: Why Most Positives Can Be False
objective: After this level you can show with a count of 10,000 people why a good test for a rare condition can give mostly false alarms.
summary: Count 10,000 people: with 1% sick and a 90%/90% test, 90 true positives meet 990 false alarms, so only 1 in 12 positives is real. The base rate decides.

cards.headline: A test that is right 9 times in 10 says yes. The chance it's real: 1 in 12.
cards.body: No trick and no faulty test. Just counting. Take 10,000 imaginary people and follow them through the test, the way Level 7 recommended: counts of people, not percents.

cards.headline: Step 1: start with the base rate
cards.body: Say 1% of them have a condition: 100 people out of 10,000. The other 9,900 don't. The test has 90% sensitivity, so it catches 90 of the 100 and misses 10. So far, so good.

cards.headline: Step 2: count the false alarms
cards.body: The test also has 90% specificity, so it clears 90% of the 9,900 healthy people: 8,910 of them. The other 10% get a false alarm. That is 990 people told they might have something they don't. Notice the mismatch: 990 false alarms against 90 true catches.

cards.context: Healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones, so even a small share of them swamps the true cases. The share of real positives rises as a condition gets more common: if 1 in 10 people had it, the same test would give 900 true and 900 false positives, so 1 in 2 would be real. A positive means little until you know the base rate.

cards.headline: False positives: counted
learned: 90 true vs 990 false: 1 in 12 positives real

questions.prompt: In the 10,000-person example, _____ of the 1,080 positive results were real.

options.rationale: 100 people had the condition, but the test missed 10 of them.
That would be half; the real share was far smaller.

questions.prompt: Follow 10,000 people through the test. Match each group with its count.
questions.explanation: 100 people have a condition and the test catches 90 of them. It also gives 990 false alarms, so there are 1,080 positives, and only 90 are real.

questions.prompt: Using the same test, what happens to the share of positive results that are real if the condition is common instead of rare?

options.label: It stays the same, since the test hasn't changed
options.rationale: The test is the same, but the base rate isn't.

options.label: It falls
options.rationale: More true cases means more true positives among the positives.

options.label: It drops to zero
options.rationale: At 1 in 10, half the positives were real.

questions.explanation: The base rate matters: at 1 in 100, 1 in 12 positives were real; at 1 in 10, 1 in 2.
